newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia sees increase in '97 wheat production.
newsitem.headline: Croatia sees increase in '97 wheat production.

text.p: Croatia has sown grain on 285,324 hectares, or 2.2 percent up on 1996, and will for the first time in years sow and harvest in the last Serb enclave on its soil, the ministry of agriculture said on Tuesday.

Current estimates put the wheat harvest this summer at some 820,000 tonnes, or 10.5 percent more than in 1996, said deputy minister Vlado Bicanic. The figures do not include the Eastern Slavonia enclave, ruled by a provisional U.N. administration.

Some 29,000 hectares sown in the fertile plains of Eastern Slavonia are expected to yield some 110,000 tonnes of wheat, maize, barley and rape, Bicanic said. But harvesting there is fraught with problems, caused by lingering ethnic mistrust.

The enclave broke away in 1991, opposing Zagreb's secession from federal Yugoslavia. The U.N. administration's current mandate expires on July 15 and Croatia has already began introducing its political and economic system into the easternmost region, bordering Serbia.

The Croatian Chamber of commerce (HGK) and the Ministry said earlier Croatia's domestic needs amounted to some 550,000 tonnes. They also warned wheat production had been gradually declining since the country gained independence in 1991.

Last year's harvest was marred by farmers' refusal to sell wheat at a purchase price lower than that earlier guaranteed by the government. This eventually forced Croatia to make expensive import from the U.S. and Argentina.
Bicanic said the guaranteed price of 1.1 kuna per kilo, the same as last year, would be firmly observed by the government.
"The (purchase) price of 1.1 kuna is guaranteed. That's the minimum price and if someone wants to pay more they are free to do so," he said.

Responding to reports that some militant Serbs in Eastern Slavonia have threatened to set fire to the crops or smuggle the harvest to nearby Yugoslavia, rather than turn it in to government silos, Bicanic said, "Croatian government has assumed responsibility to buy the wheat at a guaranteed price, which is the same for the whole of Croatia and is certainly higher than that in Serbia. But we must also have mechanisms to prevent illegal export (to Yugoslavia)."
Croatia would ask the U.N. and the joint Croat-Serb police units to monitor the enclave's borders with Yugoslavia and would also urge all farmers, Croats and Serbs alike, to inspect crops for fire.

The government will also ask U.N. Administrator Jacques Klein to issue special passes for Croatian workers and combines that will take part in harvesting so that they could freely cross the U.N.-patrolled lines, Bicanic said.
